title: Trump announces 100% tariff on branded and patented drug imports
description_medium: On September 25, 2025, President Donald Trump announced a 100% tariff on imported branded and patented pharmaceutical products, scheduled to begin October 1. He said companies with drug-manufacturing plants under construction in the United States would be exempt. Trump framed the measure as an incentive to move production to the country. The linked CNBC report covers pharmaceuticals; it does not substantiate tariffs on trucks or furniture.
description_long: President Donald Trump announced on September 25, 2025, that the United States would impose a 100% tariff on imported branded or patented pharmaceutical products starting October 1. He said companies building manufacturing plants in the United States would not face the tariff, including firms whose projects were already underway. Trump described the policy as a way to encourage drugmakers to manufacture domestically. CNBC reported that U.S. pharmaceutical imports were worth about $213 billion in 2024 and summarized industry concerns that a tariff could increase costs, complicate supply chains or alter investment decisions. Those were projections rather than effects already measured after implementation. Trump had previously discussed tariffs of up to 250%, but the September announcement specified a 100% rate. The material supports the pharmaceutical tariff and its construction-based exemption. A short description in the record also groups this announcement with levies on large trucks and furniture, but the linked reporting does not cover those products or their terms. Those measures need their own sources before they can be included as part of the same announcement.
evidence_notes: CNBC supports the drug tariff rate, effective date, exemption and estimated import value. No source here for other product tariffs.
corrected_wording: Limit this entry to the announced pharmaceutical tariff and its exemption; source truck/furniture tariffs separately.

title: DHS says SEVIS termination does not itself end a student’s immigration status
description_medium: In spring 2025, federal court filings said that terminating a student’s SEVIS database record did not by itself end the student’s nonimmigrant status. The clarification came amid widespread record terminations that left international students uncertain about enrollment and deportation risk. Reporting documented hundreds of affected students and university disruptions, while later court proceedings led DHS to restore many records temporarily as it developed a policy. The supplied headline’s “tricked” and “hundreds of thousands” claims are unsupported.
description_long: In early 2025, Immigration and Customs Enforcement terminated international students’ records in the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System, or SEVIS, after background checks and visa reviews. The record terminations caused confusion because colleges use SEVIS to track students’ visa-related enrollment, and some schools responded by removing students from classes or advising them to leave the country. During litigation over the policy, the government argued that a SEVIS termination did not necessarily mean that a student’s nonimmigrant status had ended. A court filing likewise noted that database status and immigration status were not automatically identical. Reuters later reported that more than 4,700 student records had been removed since Trump took office, according to the American Immigration Lawyers Association, and that the administration planned to restore hundreds of affected records while developing a new policy. The episode involved students, universities, immigration officials and multiple court cases. The available evidence does not show DHS describing its approach as a “trick,” and reports count thousands, not hundreds of thousands, of records. The department’s stated legal position and the real disruptions to students can both be described without treating the exaggerated headline as fact.
evidence_notes: Court filing states SEVIS termination does not necessarily terminate status. Reuters reports more than 4,700 records since Jan. 20 and restoration of hundreds pending new guidance; no evidence for 'tricked' or 100,000s.

title: Trump orders National Guard deployment to Portland, calling it “war-ravaged”
description_medium: On September 27, 2025, Trump said he would send “all necessary Troops” to Portland and described the city as “war-ravaged,” citing protests near an ICE facility. Oregon and Portland challenged the order. A federal judge initially blocked deployment, finding the protests had not been significantly violent or disruptive before Trump’s directive; the administration also sent California National Guard troops, prompting another court order. The sources document a contested deployment effort, not an uncontested military occupation of Portland.
description_long: President Donald Trump announced on September 27, 2025, that he would send “all necessary Troops” to Portland, Oregon, to protect federal property, and described the city as “war-ravaged.” His administration ordered the federalization of 200 members of the Oregon National Guard for the mission, despite objections from state and city leaders. Oregon and Portland sued, arguing that the protests at an ICE facility did not meet the legal conditions for federalizing the Guard. A federal judge temporarily blocked the deployment, citing evidence that demonstrations had not been significantly violent or disruptive in the period before Trump’s directive. The administration then sent California National Guard members toward Portland, and the judge extended the block to troops from other states. Later litigation continued over the president’s authority and the deployment. Portland’s official timeline says Oregon National Guard troops were never lawfully deployed to the city. The event is therefore an order and ensuing effort to send troops, challenged in court, rather than a completed military occupation. Trump’s “war-ravaged” description was his characterization; it was not the court’s finding about conditions in Portland.
evidence_notes: City/court timeline distinguishes Trump’s announcement, federal orders, injunctions and the fact Oregon troops were not lawfully deployed. Avoid treating the announcement as completed deployment.

title: DHS spokesperson warns more arrests may follow Newark ICE-facility confrontation
description_medium: After ICE arrested Newark Mayor Ras Baraka at Delaney Hall on May 9, 2025, three Democratic members of Congress who were visiting the facility became involved in a confrontation with federal agents. The next day, DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin told CNN, “There will be more arrests coming.” She did not name lawmakers or specify who would be arrested. Representative LaMonica McIver was later charged, but the remark itself was a prediction, not an arrest order.
description_long: On May 9, 2025, ICE agents arrested Newark Mayor Ras Baraka during a visit by three Democratic members of Congress to Delaney Hall, a privately operated immigration detention center. The lawmakers—Representatives Bonnie Watson Coleman, LaMonica McIver and Rob Menendez—were there for an oversight visit. A tense exchange followed as federal agents and the lawmakers disputed what happened at the facility gate. The next morning, DHS spokesperson Tricia McLaughlin told CNN that “there will be more arrests coming,” referring to the incident. She did not identify people as targets or outline a plan for additional arrests. Baraka was charged with trespassing and later had the charge dismissed. McIver was subsequently indicted over the confrontation, a separate legal development that came after McLaughlin’s statement. The remark drew scrutiny because it suggested possible enforcement against elected officials following their attempt to inspect a detention facility. It should be reported as the spokesperson’s warning at that time, not as evidence that arrests had already occurred or that DHS had announced a general policy toward Democratic lawmakers.
evidence_notes: Politico reports McLaughlin’s exact CNN statement; Reuters describes the facility visit and Baraka arrest. Subsequent charges should not be projected backward as a direct DHS arrest announcement.

title: Gabbard dismisses intelligence officials after council memo challenges deportation rationale
description_medium: Director of National Intelligence Tulsi Gabbard dismissed National Intelligence Council acting chair Michael Collins and deputy Maria Langan-Riekhof in May 2025, about a week after the council released a declassified assessment that contradicted the administration’s claims about Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua gang. Gabbard’s office said the officials opposed President Trump, without giving examples. Both had more than 25 years of intelligence experience. The available sources do not establish that their dismissals were illegal.
description_long: Tulsi Gabbard, the director of national intelligence, dismissed Michael Collins, acting chair of the National Intelligence Council, and his deputy Maria Langan-Riekhof in May 2025. The decision came about a week after a declassified council assessment contradicted the Trump administration’s assertions that Venezuela’s government had directed the Tren de Aragua gang. The administration had cited those claims when invoking the Alien Enemies Act to remove Venezuelan migrants. Gabbard’s office told the Associated Press that the two officials were dismissed because they opposed President Trump, but it did not provide examples. Collins and Langan-Riekhof each had more than 25 years of intelligence experience. The National Intelligence Council synthesizes intelligence from across agencies into assessments for senior national-security officials. Gabbard also announced that the council and staff preparing the President’s Daily Brief would move from CIA facilities to the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, giving her office more direct control over those functions. The timing renewed debate about political pressure on intelligence analysis. The reporting supports the dismissals and their context, but does not establish that they were unlawful or that the officials were fired solely over one report.
evidence_notes: AP reports Gabbard’s office stated opposition to Trump as reason; chronology links firings with a contradictory NIC assessment. No finding of illegal firing.

title: MAHA report cited nonexistent studies and had other citation errors
description_medium: The Make America Healthy Again report released by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. in May 2025 cited several studies that researchers and reporters could not locate, including references about children’s mental health, ADHD-drug advertising and asthma treatment. HHS revised or replaced multiple citations after the errors became public. The department called them citation and formatting errors and said the report’s conclusions were unchanged. Reporting identified specific citation problems; it did not show that every study in the report was fabricated.
description_long: On May 22, 2025, Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. released the Make America Healthy Again report on chronic disease among U.S. children. Within days, reporters and researchers found references that did not correspond to real publications or misrepresented the work of named scholars. Examples included a purported study on adolescent mental health, articles said to address direct-to-consumer advertising of ADHD drugs, and a citation about overprescribing asthma medication. Researchers whose names appeared in the report said they had not written the cited studies or that the report overstated their findings. The Department of Health and Human Services revised citations after questions were raised; by May 30, Columbia’s Sabin Center counted at least 18 citations changed or replaced. HHS described the issues as minor citation and formatting errors and said the report’s substance remained the same. The controversy concerned the reliability of the report’s references and the claims those references were used to support. It does not establish that all studies cited in the report were nonexistent, and citation corrections do not by themselves resolve the report’s broader scientific conclusions.
evidence_notes: Guardian and PolitiFact identify nonexistent studies; Columbia documents at least 18 citations changed/replaced by May 30. Avoid blanket claim that all sources were fake.

title: Trump Organization breaks ground on proposed $1.5 billion Vietnam resort
description_medium: On May 21, 2025, Eric Trump attended a groundbreaking ceremony outside Hanoi for a proposed $1.5 billion Trump Organization development with three golf courses and a luxury residential resort. Vietnamese Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh urged local authorities to facilitate the project and said Eric Trump’s visit motivated officials to expedite it. The ceremony documents a business project involving the president’s family and a foreign government; the available reporting does not establish a bribe or improper exchange.
description_long: The Trump Organization held a groundbreaking ceremony on May 21, 2025, for a planned luxury development in Khoai Chau district outside Hanoi. Eric Trump, executive vice president of the family company, attended alongside Vietnamese Prime Minister Pham Minh Chinh. Reuters described the proposal as a $1.5 billion, 990-hectare project that would include three 18-hole golf courses and residential properties, with completion targeted for the end of 2027. Chinh said Eric Trump’s visit had motivated officials to expedite the project and urged local authorities to support its completion. The ceremony occurred as Vietnam and the United States were engaged in trade talks and as Trump’s administration was imposing tariffs on Vietnamese goods. A foreign government’s public support for a family business project can raise conflict-of-interest questions, but the event reporting does not show a payment to the Trump family in exchange for government action. It also does not detail permits, financing or contractual terms. The available facts establish the project proposal and official participation, not bribery. Any claim of an improper exchange requires evidence beyond the ceremonial appearance and the prime minister’s remarks.
evidence_notes: Reuters reports project scale, ceremony, participants and PM remarks; no evidence in this record establishes a bribe or quid pro quo.

title: OPM hiring plan asks applicants how they would advance presidential policies
description_medium: A May 29, 2025 Office of Personnel Management memo directed agencies to include four short essay questions in competitive-service job announcements at GS-5 and above. One asked how applicants would help advance the president’s executive orders and policy priorities in the role. The plan framed the question as part of a merit-hiring process, but the available memo does not require applicants to profess personal or partisan loyalty. Later guidance said answers would not be scored or required.
description_long: The Office of Personnel Management and White House Domestic Policy Council issued a Merit Hiring Plan on May 29, 2025, directing agencies to include four short essay questions in competitive-service vacancy announcements for positions graded GS-5 and above. One question asks, “How would you help advance the President’s Executive Orders and policy priorities in this role?” Applicants are also asked to identify relevant initiatives and explain how they would implement them. The plan was issued under Trump’s broader effort to change the federal hiring process and promote what the administration called merit-based recruitment. Critics argued that asking job seekers to explain how they would advance the president’s agenda could politicize hiring or operate as a loyalty test. The wording focuses on carrying out policies in the job rather than expressly requiring personal or partisan support. Subsequent OPM guidance clarified that applicants would not be disqualified for leaving the essays unanswered and that the responses should not be scored. The original memo supports describing a required essay question about presidential priorities; it does not alone establish that applicants were asked to pledge allegiance or that hiring decisions had already been based on political loyalty.
evidence_notes: OPM memo includes executive-orders question; later OPM guidance states responses would not be required/scored, correcting frozen wording on mandatory support.
